title: Chukat: look up (Numbers 21:4–9)
hook: looking at the copper serpent heals; the Mishnah says it was turning hearts toward heaven (Rosh Hashanah 3:8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron died on Mount Hor, and all the house of Israel wept thirty days for the man who pursued peace. Your line was all the house wept. Who's the peacemaker you remembered? Day four hundred sixty.

How much of your day is spent looking down? At a phone, a keyboard, a sink full of dishes, the next step on the sidewalk. Your neck probably knows the answer better than you do. The Torah has a story where looking up is the cure, quite literally. The people are walking the long way around the land of Edom. They're tired, they're sick of the manna, and they complain again. And then the snakes come.
screen: `HOW MUCH OF YOUR DAY IS LOOKING DOWN?` → `THE LONG WAY AROUND EDOM.` → `THEN THE SNAKES COME.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, it goes like this. Fiery serpents bite the people, and many die. The people come to Moses and say, we've sinned; pray that the snakes go away. Moses prays. And God's answer is not to remove the snakes. Instead: make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "every one that is bitten, when he seeth it, shall live." Moses makes a serpent of copper and raises it high, and whoever is bitten looks at it and lives. In Hebrew there's a little echo: a nachash, a serpent, made of nechoshet, copper. The rabbis were uneasy about this. A metal snake that heals? In the Mishnah, tractate Rosh Hashanah, they ask, in paraphrase: does a serpent kill, or a serpent bring life? No. When Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven, they were healed; and if not, they wasted away. So the object isn't the point. The looking up is. The Mishnah says the same about Moses' raised hands in the battle with Amalek: the hands didn't win the war; the people looking up did. And the serpent has a second life. It was kept, and the book of Kings says that in the days of King Hezekiah people were burning incense to it, and calling it Nehushtan. Hezekiah smashed it to pieces. The sign that once pointed upward had become something people stared at instead. Look up, the Mishnah says, not at the pole.
screen: `A SERPENT ON A POLE.` · `NACHASH, NECHOSHET: SERPENT, COPPER.` · `WHEN THEY LOOKED UPWARD, THEY HEALED.` · `HEZEKIAH SMASHES NEHUSHTAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up for one minute. If you can, step outside or go to a window. If not, simply raise your eyes to the highest point in the room. Let your chin lift a little and your shoulders drop. Look at the sky, or the ceiling, or the top of a tree. Notice how far up it goes. Breathe slowly. If you pray, this is a natural moment to turn your heart upward, the way the Mishnah describes. If you don't, just let your gaze rest somewhere higher than your worries. Stay there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chukat. The portion where a copper serpent on a pole heals those who look up, and the Mishnah says it was the looking up that healed.
Your line: look up and live. Today, three times, when you catch yourself looking down at a screen, lift your eyes for one full breath. Day four hundred sixty.

howItsDone: The copper serpent is read in the portion of Chukat, and the Mishnah's teaching about it, that healing came when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to heaven, is often studied alongside it.

myth: God answered Moses' prayer by removing the snakes
the snakes stayed. Moses made a copper serpent, and whoever looked at it lived.
the Mishnah says the serpent itself had healing power
it says the people healed when they looked upward and turned their hearts to heaven.
the copper serpent was later destroyed by a king of Judah
Hezekiah smashed it because people were burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4).

fork.setup: you're King Hezekiah. the copper serpent Moses made has been kept all this time, and people are burning incense to it. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Hezekiah broke it in pieces. the sign that once pointed upward had become something people worshiped.

original.note: Hebrew: a serpent of copper (Numbers 21:9), a play between nachash, serpent, and nechoshet, copper.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic snake on a stick.
what it means: a sign that pointed people upward, and healed those who looked.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8 says the serpent neither killed nor gave life, and 2 Kings 18:4 records Hezekiah destroying it when it became an object of worship.

sources.quoted: every one that is bitten, when he seeth it, shall live.

notes: Numbers 21:8 JPS 1917 'every one that is bitten, when he seeth it, shall live'; confirm.
JPS 1917 renders nechoshet as 'brass'; the script says copper, following the index. Copper/bronze both defensible.
Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8 paraphrased (serpent, and Moses' hands in Exodus 17:11).
The fork's 'answer' follows what the text reports Hezekiah did.
